claim: Activation of Wnt signaling in hPSC-derived naïve endothelial progenitors leads to robust acquisition of canonical BBB phenotypes including expression of GLUT-1.

claim: CNS vascular endothelial cells have complex tight junctions.
source: In the central nervous system (CNS), vascular endothelial cells (ECs) are highly specialized, with complex tight junctions, expression of a spectrum of nutrient and efflux transporters, low rates of vesicle trafficking, no fenestrae, and low expression of immune cell adhesion molecules (Reese and Karnovsky, 1967; Obermeier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Reese and Karnovsky, 1967; Obermeier et al., 2013).

claim: The Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway drives CNS angiogenesis during development.
source: During development, the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway drives both CNS angiogenesis, during which vascular sprouts originating from the perineural vascular plexus invade the developing neural tube, and the coupled process of barriergenesis by which resulting ECs begin to acquire BBB properties (Liebner et al., 2008; Stenman et al., 2008; Daneman et al., 2009; Engelhardt and Liebner, 2014; Umans et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature (Liebner et al., 2008; Stenman et al., 2008; Daneman et al., 2009; Engelhardt and Liebner, 2014; Umans et al., 2017).

claim: Wnt signaling upregulates multiple necessary components of the CNS EC bicellular and tricellular junctions.

evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CHIR upregulates claudin-5 (bicellular) and LSR (tricellular).

claim: CHIR treatment does not change the geometric mean dextran signal in ECs incubated at 37°C compared to DMSO.
source: In ECs incubated at 37°C, CHIR treatment did not change the geometric mean dextran signal compared to DMSO (Figure 5B and C), but did cause a broadening of the distribution of dextran intensities as quantified by the coefficient of variation (CV), indicative of subpopulations of cells with decreased and increased dextran uptake (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: CHIR treatment causes a broadening of the distribution of dextran intensities in ECs, indicative of subpopulations of cells with decreased and increased dextran uptake.
source: In ECs incubated at 37°C, CHIR treatment did not change the geometric mean dextran signal compared to DMSO (Figure 5B and C), but did cause a broadening of the distribution of dextran intensities as quantified by the coefficient of variation (CV), indicative of subpopulations of cells with decreased and increased dextran uptake (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 5B and D.

claim: Chlorpromazine (inhibitor of clathrin-mediated endocytosis) decreases dextran uptake in ECs.
source: Compared to vehicle control, chlorpromazine (inhibitor of clathrin-mediated endocytosis) and rottlerin (inhibitor of macropinocytosis) both decreased dextran uptake, while nystatin (inhibitor of caveolin-mediated endocytosis) did not significantly affect uptake (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C), consistent with the very small number of dextran+ caveolin-1+ puncta observed by confocal imaging (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Rottlerin (inhibitor of macropinocytosis) decreases dextran uptake in ECs.
source: Compared to vehicle control, chlorpromazine (inhibitor of clathrin-mediated endocytosis) and rottlerin (inhibitor of macropinocytosis) both decreased dextran uptake, while nystatin (inhibitor of caveolin-mediated endocytosis) did not significantly affect uptake (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C), consistent with the very small number of dextran+ caveolin-1+ puncta observed by confocal imaging (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Nystatin (inhibitor of caveolin-mediated endocytosis) does not significantly affect dextran uptake in ECs.
source: Compared to vehicle control, chlorpromazine (inhibitor of clathrin-mediated endocytosis) and rottlerin (inhibitor of macropinocytosis) both decreased dextran uptake, while nystatin (inhibitor of caveolin-mediated endocytosis) did not significantly affect uptake (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C), consistent with the very small number of dextran+ caveolin-1+ puncta observed by confocal imaging (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: CHIR increases the heterogeneity of the EC population with respect to the rate of endocytosis.
source: Thus, despite the generally uniform elevation of caveolin-1 and decrease of PLVAP observed by immunocytochemistry in CHIR-treated ECs, our functional assay suggests neither an overall increase nor decrease in total fluid-phase endocytosis. Instead, it indicates that CHIR increases the heterogeneity of the EC population with respect to the rate of endocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CHIR increases the coefficient of variation of dextran uptake without changing the mean.

claim: CHIR-treated Passage 3 ECs have elevated transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER).
source: CHIR-treated Passage 3 ECs had elevated transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Figure 5E) and decreased permeability to the small molecule tracer sodium fluorescein (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CHIR-treated Passage 3 ECs have decreased permeability to the small molecule tracer sodium fluorescein.
source: CHIR-treated Passage 3 ECs had elevated transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Figure 5E) and decreased permeability to the small molecule tracer sodium fluorescein (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claim: CHIR treatment initiated immediately after MACS leads to marked increase in GLUT-1 abundance in Passage 1 ECs.
source: Compared to DMSO controls, the CHIR-treated Passage 5 ECs exhibited no increase in GLUT-1 abundance (Figure 6B–D), which contrasts with the marked increase observed when CHIR treatment was initiated immediately after MACS (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: CHIR-treated Passage 5 ECs exhibit no increase in GLUT-1 abundance compared to DMSO controls.
source: Compared to DMSO controls, the CHIR-treated Passage 5 ECs exhibited no increase in GLUT-1 abundance (Figure 6B–D), which contrasts with the marked increase observed when CHIR treatment was initiated immediately after MACS (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: CHIR treatment in matured ECs (Passage 5) does not increase claudin-5 expression.
source: Furthermore, CHIR treatment in matured ECs did not increase claudin-5 expression and did not increase EC number (Figure 6B–D), in contrast to the increases observed in both properties when treatment was initiated immediately after MACS (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: CHIR treatment in matured ECs (Passage 5) does not increase EC number.
source: Furthermore, CHIR treatment in matured ECs did not increase claudin-5 expression and did not increase EC number (Figure 6B–D), in contrast to the increases observed in both properties when treatment was initiated immediately after MACS (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: Early, naïve endothelial progenitors are more responsive to Wnt activation than more mature ECs derived by the same differentiation protocol.
source: Together, these data suggest that early, naïve endothelial progenitors are more responsive to Wnt activation than more mature ECs derived by the same differentiation protocol.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of CHIR effects in Passage 1 versus Passage 5 ECs shown in Figure 6.

claim: Canonical endothelial marker genes (including CDH5, CD34, PECAM1, CLDN5, ERG, and FLI1) are enriched in ECs compared to SMLCs.
source: We next validated the endothelial identity of our cells; we observed that canonical endothelial marker genes (including CDH5, CD34, PECAM1, CLDN5, ERG, and FLI1) were enriched in ECs compared to SMLCs and had high absolute abundance, on the order of 100–1000 transcripts per million (TPM) (Figure 7B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: SMLCs express mesenchymal (mural/fibroblast)-related transcripts (including PDGFRB, CSPG4, PDGFRA, TBX2, CNN1, and COL1A1).
source: SMLCs expressed mesenchymal (mural/fibroblast)-related transcripts (including PDGFRB, CSPG4, PDGFRA, TBX2, CNN1, and COL1A1), which ECs generally lacked, although we did observe slight enrichment of some of these genes in Passage 1 DMSO-treated ECs, likely reflective of a small amount of SMLC contamination despite CD31 FACS (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: ECs have little to no expression of epithelial genes CDH1, EPCAM, CLDN1, CLDN3, CLDN4, and CLDN6.
source: We also observed little to no expression of the epithelial genes CDH1, EPCAM, CLDN1, CLDN3 (Castro Dias et al., 2019), CLDN4, and CLDN6, reflecting the definitive endothelial nature of the cells (Figure 7B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 1369 genes are significantly upregulated in Passage 1 CHIR-treated ECs compared to DMSO-treated ECs.
source: First comparing CHIR- and DMSO-treated ECs at Passage 1, we identified 1369 significantly upregulated genes and 2037 significantly downregulated genes (Figure 7C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: 2037 genes are significantly downregulated in Passage 1 CHIR-treated ECs compared to DMSO-treated ECs.
source: First comparing CHIR- and DMSO-treated ECs at Passage 1, we identified 1369 significantly upregulated genes and 2037 significantly downregulated genes (Figure 7C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: CHIR upregulates SLC2A1, CLDN5, LSR, and CAV1 in Passage 1 ECs.
source: CHIR-upregulated genes included SLC2A1, CLDN5, LSR, and CAV1, consistent with protein-level assays.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data and is consistent with protein-level data shown in earlier figures.

claim: CHIR downregulates PLVAP in Passage 1 ECs.
source: PLVAP was downregulated, as were a number of mesenchymal genes (TAGLN, COL1A1), again reflective of slight contamination of SMLC transcripts in the DMSO-treated EC samples (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: CHIR upregulates LEF1 and TCF7 in Passage 1 ECs.
source: Additionally, important downstream effectors of Wnt signaling were upregulated, including the transcription factors LEF1 and TCF7, the negative regulator AXIN2, and the negative regulator APCDD1, which is known to modulate Wnt-regulated barriergenesis in retinal endothelium (Mazzoni et al., 2017; Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: CHIR upregulates AXIN2 in Passage 1 ECs.
source: Additionally, important downstream effectors of Wnt signaling were upregulated, including the transcription factors LEF1 and TCF7, the negative regulator AXIN2, and the negative regulator APCDD1, which is known to modulate Wnt-regulated barriergenesis in retinal endothelium (Mazzoni et al., 2017; Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: CHIR upregulates APCDD1 in Passage 1 ECs.
source: Additionally, important downstream effectors of Wnt signaling were upregulated, including the transcription factors LEF1 and TCF7, the negative regulator AXIN2, and the negative regulator APCDD1, which is known to modulate Wnt-regulated barriergenesis in retinal endothelium (Mazzoni et al., 2017; Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: APCDD1 is known to modulate Wnt-regulated barriergenesis in retinal endothelium.
source: Additionally, important downstream effectors of Wnt signaling were upregulated, including the transcription factors LEF1 and TCF7, the negative regulator AXIN2, and the negative regulator APCDD1, which is known to modulate Wnt-regulated barriergenesis in retinal endothelium (Mazzoni et al., 2017; Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Mazzoni et al., 2017).

claim: CHIR upregulates ZIC3 in Passage 1 ECs.
source: We also identified upregulated transcription factors: ZIC3, which is highly enriched in brain and retinal ECs in vivo and downstream of Frizzled4 signaling (Wang et al., 2012; Sabbagh et al., 2018), and SOX7, which acts cooperatively with SOX17 and SOX18 in retinal angiogenesis (Zhou et al., 2015), were upregulated by CHIR in our system (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: ZIC3 is highly enriched in brain and retinal ECs in vivo and downstream of Frizzled4 signaling.
source: We also identified upregulated transcription factors: ZIC3, which is highly enriched in brain and retinal ECs in vivo and downstream of Frizzled4 signaling (Wang et al., 2012; Sabbagh et al., 2018), and SOX7, which acts cooperatively with SOX17 and SOX18 in retinal angiogenesis (Zhou et al., 2015), were upregulated by CHIR in our system (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Wang et al., 2012; Sabbagh et al., 2018).

claim: CHIR upregulates SOX7 in Passage 1 ECs.
source: We also identified upregulated transcription factors: ZIC3, which is highly enriched in brain and retinal ECs in vivo and downstream of Frizzled4 signaling (Wang et al., 2012; Sabbagh et al., 2018), and SOX7, which acts cooperatively with SOX17 and SOX18 in retinal angiogenesis (Zhou et al., 2015), were upregulated by CHIR in our system (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: SOX7 acts cooperatively with SOX17 and SOX18 in retinal angiogenesis.
source: We also identified upregulated transcription factors: ZIC3, which is highly enriched in brain and retinal ECs in vivo and downstream of Frizzled4 signaling (Wang et al., 2012; Sabbagh et al., 2018), and SOX7, which acts cooperatively with SOX17 and SOX18 in retinal angiogenesis (Zhou et al., 2015), were upregulated by CHIR in our system (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Zhou et al., 2015).

claim: CHIR upregulates MSX1 and EBF1 in Passage 1 ECs.
source: MSX1 and EBF1, which are expressed by murine brain ECs in vivo (Vanlandewijck et al., 2018), were also CHIR-upregulated (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: MSX1 and EBF1 are expressed by murine brain ECs in vivo.
source: MSX1 and EBF1, which are expressed by murine brain ECs in vivo (Vanlandewijck et al., 2018), were also CHIR-upregulated (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Vanlandewijck et al., 2018).

claim: CHIR upregulates ABCG2 in Passage 1 ECs.
source: Additional CHIR-upregulated genes included ABCG2 (encoding the efflux transporter breast cancer resistance protein [BCRP]), APLN, a tip cell marker enriched in postnatal day 7 murine brain ECs compared to those of other organs, and subsequently downregulated in adulthood (Sabbagh et al., 2018; Sabbagh and Nathans, 2020), and FLVCR2, a disease-associated gene with a recently identified role in brain angiogenesis (Santander et al., 2020; Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: CHIR upregulates APLN in Passage 1 ECs.
source: Additional CHIR-upregulated genes included ABCG2 (encoding the efflux transporter breast cancer resistance protein [BCRP]), APLN, a tip cell marker enriched in postnatal day 7 murine brain ECs compared to those of other organs, and subsequently downregulated in adulthood (Sabbagh et al., 2018; Sabbagh and Nathans, 2020), and FLVCR2, a disease-associated gene with a recently identified role in brain angiogenesis (Santander et al., 2020; Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: APLN is a tip cell marker enriched in postnatal day 7 murine brain ECs compared to those of other organs, and subsequently downregulated in adulthood.
source: Additional CHIR-upregulated genes included ABCG2 (encoding the efflux transporter breast cancer resistance protein [BCRP]), APLN, a tip cell marker enriched in postnatal day 7 murine brain ECs compared to those of other organs, and subsequently downregulated in adulthood (Sabbagh et al., 2018; Sabbagh and Nathans, 2020), and FLVCR2, a disease-associated gene with a recently identified role in brain angiogenesis (Santander et al., 2020; Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Sabbagh et al., 2018; Sabbagh and Nathans, 2020).

source: Additional CHIR-upregulated genes included ABCG2 (encoding the efflux transporter breast cancer resistance protein [BCRP]), APLN, a tip cell marker enriched in postnatal day 7 murine brain ECs compared to those of other organs, and subsequently downregulated in adulthood (Sabbagh et al., 2018; Sabbagh and Nathans, 2020), and FLVCR2, a disease-associated gene with a recently identified role in brain angiogenesis (Santander et al., 2020; Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: FLVCR2 is a disease-associated gene with a recently identified role in brain angiogenesis.
source: Additional CHIR-upregulated genes included ABCG2 (encoding the efflux transporter breast cancer resistance protein [BCRP]), APLN, a tip cell marker enriched in postnatal day 7 murine brain ECs compared to those of other organs, and subsequently downregulated in adulthood (Sabbagh et al., 2018; Sabbagh and Nathans, 2020), and FLVCR2, a disease-associated gene with a recently identified role in brain angiogenesis (Santander et al., 2020; Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Santander et al., 2020).

claim: CHIR downregulates FABP4 in Passage 1 ECs.
source: Finally, we detected CHIR-mediated downregulation of the fatty acid-binding protein-encoding FABP4, which is depleted in brain ECs compared to those of peripheral organs (Sabbagh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data.

claim: FABP4 is depleted in brain ECs compared to those of peripheral organs.
source: Finally, we detected CHIR-mediated downregulation of the fatty acid-binding protein-encoding FABP4, which is depleted in brain ECs compared to those of peripheral organs (Sabbagh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Sabbagh et al., 2018).

claim: CHIR downregulates SMAD6 in Passage 1 ECs.
source: We also observed similar downregulation of SMAD6, which is depleted in brain ECs compared to lung ECs and is a putative negative regulator of BMP-mediated angiogenesis (Mouillesseaux et al., 2016; Vanlandewijck et al., 2018; Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: SMAD6 is depleted in brain ECs compared to lung ECs and is a putative negative regulator of BMP-mediated angiogenesis.
source: We also observed similar downregulation of SMAD6, which is depleted in brain ECs compared to lung ECs and is a putative negative regulator of BMP-mediated angiogenesis (Mouillesseaux et al., 2016; Vanlandewijck et al., 2018; Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Mouillesseaux et al., 2016; Vanlandewijck et al., 2018).

claim: Many CHIR-mediated gene expression changes observed at Passage 1 persist in Passage 3 ECs, including SLC2A1, LSR, LEF1, AXIN2, APCDD1, ZIC3, EBF1, FLVCR2, and ABCG2 upregulation and PLVAP downregulation.
source: In Passage 3 ECs, many of the CHIR-mediated gene expression changes observed at Passage 1 persisted, including SLC2A1, LSR, LEF1, AXIN2, APCDD1, ZIC3, EBF1, FLVCR2, and ABCG2 upregulation and PLVAP downregulation (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: At Passage 3, CLDN5 is not upregulated in CHIR-treated cells compared to DMSO-treated cells, but is highly expressed (~2500 TPM).
source: On the other hand, at Passage 3, CLDN5 was not upregulated in CHIR-treated cells compared to DMSO-treated cells, but was highly expressed (~2500 TPM).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: At Passage 3, CAV1 abundance remains high, but is not CHIR-upregulated.
source: Similarly, CAV1 abundance remained high, but was not CHIR-upregulated in Passage 3 cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: JAM2 is upregulated by CHIR at Passage 3, but not at Passage 1.
source: Conversely, JAM2, which encodes junctional adhesion molecule 2, a component of EC tight junctions (Aurrand-Lions et al., 2001; Tietz and Engelhardt, 2015), was upregulated by CHIR at Passage 3, but not at Passage 1, as was the retinol-binding protein-encoding gene RBP1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: JAM2 encodes junctional adhesion molecule 2, a component of EC tight junctions.
source: Conversely, JAM2, which encodes junctional adhesion molecule 2, a component of EC tight junctions (Aurrand-Lions et al., 2001; Tietz and Engelhardt, 2015), was upregulated by CHIR at Passage 3, but not at Passage 1, as was the retinol-binding protein-encoding gene RBP1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Aurrand-Lions et al., 2001; Tietz and Engelhardt, 2015).

claim: RBP1 is upregulated by CHIR at Passage 3, but not at Passage 1.
source: Conversely, JAM2, which encodes junctional adhesion molecule 2, a component of EC tight junctions (Aurrand-Lions et al., 2001; Tietz and Engelhardt, 2015), was upregulated by CHIR at Passage 3, but not at Passage 1, as was the retinol-binding protein-encoding gene RBP1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The green module from WGCNA has a representative gene expression profile (module eigengene) with a strong, positive correlation with CHIR treatment.
source: One such module (the green module, containing 441 genes) had a representative gene expression profile (module eigengene) with a strong, positive correlation with CHIR treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the WGCNA analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Genes central to the green module include canonical transcriptional targets of Wnt/β-catenin signaling, including AXIN2 and APCDD1.
source: Importantly, genes central to this module included canonical transcriptional targets of Wnt/β-catenin signaling, including AXIN2 and APCDD1, further supporting the key role of β-catenin signaling in transcriptional changes observed in CHIR-treated ECs.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the WGCNA analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Extended culture to Passage 3 in the absence of exogenous Wnt activation leads to 1521 upregulated genes, including CLDN5 and CAV1.
source: Extended culture to Passage 3 in the absence of exogeneous Wnt activation led to 1521 upregulated genes, including CLDN5 and CAV1, consistent with previously reported protein-level observations in EECM-BMEC-like cells (Nishihara et al., 2020), which are analogous to Passage 3 DMSO-treated cells.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: Extended culture to Passage 3 in the absence of exogenous Wnt activation leads to 1625 downregulated genes, including marked downregulation of PLVAP.
source: We also observed 1625 downregulated genes, including marked downregulation of PLVAP (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: SLC2A1 is not upregulated at Passage 3 compared to Passage 1 in DMSO-treated ECs.
source: SLC2A1, however, was not upregulated at Passage 3 (Figure 7—figure supplement 4), concordant with absence of GLUT-1 protein expression in the control ECs (Figure 6B), nor was LSR.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: LSR is not upregulated at Passage 3 compared to Passage 1 in DMSO-treated ECs.
source: SLC2A1, however, was not upregulated at Passage 3 (Figure 7—figure supplement 4), concordant with absence of GLUT-1 protein expression in the control ECs (Figure 6B), nor was LSR.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: LEF1 and TCF7 are strongly downregulated in Passage 3 DMSO-treated ECs compared to Passage 1.
source: While CTNNB1, GSK3B, and genes encoding components of the destruction complex were not significantly different between Passage 3 and Passage 1, LEF1 and TCF7 were strongly downregulated in Passage 3 cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: 130 of the brain-enriched genes are CHIR-upregulated in Passage 1 ECs.
source: Using the resulting sets of 1094 brain-enriched and 506 brain-depleted genes, we asked how many genes in our Passage 1 ECs were concordantly regulated by CHIR: 130 of the brain-enriched genes were CHIR-upregulated and 116 of the brain-depleted genes were CHIR-downregulated (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: 116 of the brain-depleted genes are CHIR-downregulated in Passage 1 ECs.
source: Using the resulting sets of 1094 brain-enriched and 506 brain-depleted genes, we asked how many genes in our Passage 1 ECs were concordantly regulated by CHIR: 130 of the brain-enriched genes were CHIR-upregulated and 116 of the brain-depleted genes were CHIR-downregulated (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: In pituitary ECs with β-catenin stabilization, 102 of the brain-enriched genes are upregulated and 48 of the brain-depleted genes are downregulated.
source: In pituitary ECs with β-catenin stabilization, 102 of the brain-enriched genes were upregulated and 48 of the brain-depleted genes were downregulated (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: In liver ECs with β-catenin stabilization, 25 brain-enriched genes are upregulated and 1 brain-depleted gene is downregulated.
source: Compared with the pituitary ECs, there were far fewer concordantly regulated genes in liver ECs with β-catenin stabilization, with 25 upregulated and 1 downregulated (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: In cultured primary mouse brain ECs with β-catenin stabilization, 72 brain-enriched genes are concordantly upregulated and 16 brain-depleted genes are concordantly downregulated.
source: Finally, cultured primary mouse brain ECs with β-catenin stabilization exhibited 72 concordantly upregulated and 16 downregulated genes (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 8F.

claim: AXIN2 is the only gene concordantly regulated in all four β-catenin activation comparisons (hPSC EC, pituitary EC, liver EC, cultured brain EC).
source: The only gene concordantly regulated in all four comparisons was the canonical Wnt target AXIN2.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 8C-F.

claim: MFSD2A is robustly upregulated by β-catenin in pituitary ECs, but not in any other context.
source: Notably, the caveolae inhibitor MFSD2A was robustly upregulated by β-catenin in pituitary ECs, but not in any other context (Figure 8C–F), suggesting that other brain-derived factors may cooperate with Wnt to regulate expression of this important inhibitor of caveolin-mediated transcytosis.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 8C–F.

claim: Other brain-derived factors may cooperate with Wnt to regulate expression of MFSD2A.
source: Notably, the caveolae inhibitor MFSD2A was robustly upregulated by β-catenin in pituitary ECs, but not in any other context (Figure 8C–F), suggesting that other brain-derived factors may cooperate with Wnt to regulate expression of this important inhibitor of caveolin-mediated transcytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MFSD2A is only upregulated in pituitary ECs in vivo, where other brain-derived factors are present.

claim: The hPSC-derived ECs responded to Wnt activation in a fashion that led to modest induction of CNS transcriptional programs.
source: In sum, the data suggest that the hPSC-derived ECs responded to Wnt activation in a fashion that led to modest induction of CNS transcriptional programs and that the response was most similar to the pituitary β-catenin stabilization model.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: The response of hPSC-derived ECs to Wnt activation is most similar to the pituitary β-catenin stabilization model.
source: In sum, the data suggest that the hPSC-derived ECs responded to Wnt activation in a fashion that led to modest induction of CNS transcriptional programs and that the response was most similar to the pituitary β-catenin stabilization model.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Immature endothelium is highly responsive to Wnt activation where mature (adult) endothelium is largely refractory except in regions proximal to barrier-forming regions.
source: Importantly, this analysis also supports the hypothesis that immature endothelium is highly responsive to Wnt activation where mature (adult) endothelium is largely refractory except in regions proximal to barrier-forming regions.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative analysis and the observation that pituitary ECs (proximal to CNS) retain some responsiveness.
